title: OpenAI slashed AI prices. Usage soared and revenue jumped.
excerpt: After OpenAI slashed AI model prices, it boosted usage and revenue, illustrating Jevons Paradox where cheaper costs drive higher consumption.
content_html:
AI prices are plunging. That feels bad, but something else is happening.

By Alistair Barr

You're currently following this author! Want to unfollow? Unsubscribe via the link in your email.

Author of the Tech Memo newsletter

The price of AI is falling fast. That might sound like bad news for the industry. Early evidence suggests the opposite is happening.

OpenAI recently slashed the price of its GPT-5.6 Luna model by 80%. It also cut the price of its mid-range Terra model by 20%.

Then something striking happened: Customers started using dramatically more AI.

TD Cowen analysts studied usage data from OpenRouter, a service that lets developers access various AI models and has lately been discounting some models, including Luna and Terra. The analysts found that the effective price of using Luna fell roughly tenfold after the cuts. Meanwhile, consumption jumped about 14-fold. Terra's effective price fell roughly threefold while usage increased about fivefold.

AI usage is commonly measured in "tokens," the small units of information that models process. Companies often pay to access AI models based on the number of tokens they consume.

The remarkable part is that usage rose faster than prices fell. TD Cowen estimated that OpenAI's revenue from Luna increased about 34% compared with the seven-day period before the price cut. Terra revenue rose about 45%.

The Luna situation is the most notable. When you slash a product's price by 80%, it's pretty unusual to actually generate more revenue.

To me, this clearly shows an idea AI executives have repeated so often that it's become an industry cliché. I've barred myself from writing about this. Now, with such fascinating data points, I'm finally going to utter the phrase: Jevons Paradox.

Yuck. I feel a bit dirty now.

Anyway, the idea dates to the 19th century, when economist William Stanley Jevons observed that improvements in the efficiency of coal use didn't reduce coal consumption. They helped increase it dramatically. Making a useful resource cheaper can encourage people to find many more uses for it.

This seems counterintuitive to many people. In Silicon Valley, it's a common assumption because it's happened again and again.

Take computers, for example. They used to be huge mainframe machines that cost an outrageous sum of money even to tap into for a few hours. Then came business computers that cost so much that only companies could afford them. Today, you can buy a smartphone for about $400, and that machine is more powerful than those old computers.

And guess what? Almost every single person on Earth uses these small computers and carries them around in their pockets. Did revenue plunge as prices slumped? No. Apple generated $109 billion in revenue in its latest quarter. That's up from just over $100 million in annual revenue when the company went public in 1980 (when computers cost a hell of a lot more).

AI could be following the same pattern.

Lower prices make it economical to put AI to work on tasks that previously weren't worth the expense. Companies can use cheaper AI models to analyze more documents, answer more customer questions, write more software, and run automated agents that perform multiple steps for every request.

Ramp found that OpenAI's GPT-5.6 Sol model captured more business spending in July than Anthropic's top Fable 5 model. That was likely because OpenAI's model is cheaper, and therefore, businesses used it more than Fable.

This dynamic is particularly important because the underlying cost of producing AI tokens is falling, too. New computing systems can generate them much more efficiently, so token prices will plunge all over again.

The TD Cowen results cover only about two weeks after OpenAI's price cuts, so it's too early to know whether the revenue bounce will last. The analysts themselves said they want to see whether the trend holds over time.

For now, the emerging lesson is simple: The cheaper AI gets, the more of it we use.

人工智能的价格正在快速下降。 对于该行业来说，这听起来可能是个坏消息。 早期证据表明相反的情况正在发生。

OpenAI 最近将其 GPT-5.6 Luna 模型的价格下调了 80%。 它还将中档 Terra 车型的价格降低了 20%。

然后发生了一些惊人的事情：客户开始使用更多的人工智能。

TD Cowen 分析师研究了 OpenRouter 的使用数据，该服务允许开发人员访问各种 AI 模型，并且最近对某些模型进行了折扣，包括 Luna 和 Terra。 分析师发现，在降价后，使用 Luna 的有效价格大约下降了十倍。 与此同时，消费量猛增约 14 倍。 Terra 的有效价格下降了大约三倍，而使用量增加了大约五倍。

人工智能的使用通常以“令牌”来衡量，即模型处理的小信息单位。 公司通常根据其消耗的代币数量付费来访问人工智能模型。

值得注意的是，使用量的增长速度快于价格的下降速度。 TD Cowen 估计 OpenAI 来自 Luna 的收入与降价前 7 天相比增长了约 34%。 Terra 收入增长约 45%。

Luna 的情况最为引人注目。 当你将产品价格削减 80% 时，实际上产生更多收入是很不寻常的。

对我来说，这清楚地表明了人工智能高管经常重复的一个想法，以至于它已经成为行业的陈词滥调。 我已经禁止自己写这个了。 现在，有了如此令人着迷的数据点，我终于要说出这句话：杰文斯悖论。

恶心。 我现在感觉有点脏。

不管怎样，这个想法可以追溯到 19 世纪，当时经济学家威廉·斯坦利·杰文斯 (William Stanley Jevons) 观察到，煤炭使用效率的提高并没有减少煤炭消耗。 他们帮助大幅增加了这一数字。 让有用的资源变得更便宜可以鼓励人们找到它的更多用途。

这对许多人来说似乎违反直觉。 在硅谷，这是一个常见的假设，因为这种情况一次又一次地发生。

以计算机为例。 它们曾经是巨大的大型机，即使使用几个小时也要花费大量金钱。 随后出现的商用计算机价格昂贵，只有公司才能买得起。 如今，你可以花大约 400 美元购买一部智能手机，而且那台机器比那些旧电脑更强大。

你猜怎么着？ 地球上几乎每个人都使用这些小型计算机并将它们放在口袋里。 收入是否随着价格下跌而大幅下降？ 不会。苹果公司最近一个季度的收入为 1090 亿美元。 这比该公司 1980 年上市时的年收入略高于 1 亿美元（当时计算机的价格要高得多）。

人工智能可能会遵循相同的模式。

较低的价格使得人工智能可以更经济地完成以前不值得花费的任务。 公司可以使用更便宜的人工智能模型来分析更多文档，回答更多客户问题，编写更多软件，并运行针对每个请求执行多个步骤的自动化代理。

Ramp 发现 OpenAI 的 GPT-5.6 Sol 模型在 7 月份捕获的业务支出比 Anthropic 的顶级 Fable 5 模型更多。 这可能是因为 OpenAI 的模型更便宜，因此企业比 Fable 使用它更多。

这种动态尤其重要，因为生产人工智能代币的基本成本也在下降。 新的计算系统可以更有效地生成它们，因此代币价格将再次暴跌。

TD Cowen 的业绩仅涵盖 OpenAI 降价后约两周的时间，因此现在判断收入反弹是否会持续还为时过早。 分析师们自己表示，他们想看看这种趋势是否会随着时间的推移而持续下去。

目前，新出现的教训很简单：人工智能越便宜，我们使用的就越多。
